phrases.translation: Alif-Lãm-Ra. ˹This is˺ a Book whose verses are well perfected and then fully explained. ˹It is˺ from the One ˹Who is˺ All-Wise, All-Aware
phrases.explanation: The surah opens with the separated letters Alif-Lãm-Ra, whose full meaning is not explained in this verse. Their sound marks the beginning of a revelation whose guidance is presented as carefully formed. The Book’s verses are perfected and fully explained, and it comes from the All-Wise, All-Aware. The opening grounds its guidance in divine wisdom and complete knowledge.

phrases.translation: ˹Tell them, O Prophet,˺ “Worship none but Allah. Surely I am a warner and deliverer of good news to you from Him
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to call people to worship Allah alone. This is the central message that shapes both the warning about wrongdoing and the good news offered to those who respond. The messenger warns people and brings good news from Allah. His role is to convey both accountability and hope, rather than to force anyone to believe.

phrases.translation: And seek your Lord’s forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance. He will grant you a good provision for an appointed term and graciously reward the doers of good.
phrases.explanation: People are asked to seek forgiveness and turn back to Allah. Repentance means changing direction after wrongdoing, not merely asking to escape consequences while continuing the same conduct. Allah promises good provision for an appointed term and a gracious reward to those who do good. The verse joins worldly provision with moral effort and lasting reward.

phrases.translation: But if you turn away, then I truly fear for you the torment of a formidable Day
phrases.explanation: Those who turn away face a warning of a formidable Day. The Prophet expresses concern for them because rejection does not remove the reality of their eventual return and accountability.

phrases.translation: To Allah is your return. And He is Most Capable of everything.”
phrases.explanation: Everyone returns to Allah, who is capable of everything. The statement places the whole human journey under His authority and assures the audience that no person or deed is beyond His power.

phrases.translation: Indeed, they enfold ˹what is in˺ their hearts, ˹trying˺ to hide it from Him!
phrases.explanation: Some people conceal what is in their hearts, as though hiding inward thoughts from Allah were possible. The verse challenges the attempt to escape divine knowledge through outward coverings or secrecy.

phrases.translation: But even when they cover themselves with their clothes, He knows what they conceal and what they reveal. Surely He knows best what is ˹hidden˺ in the heart
phrases.explanation: Allah knows what people hide and what they show, even when they cover themselves with clothing. Their public appearance cannot conceal private intentions from Him. Allah knows best what is hidden in the heart. This complete knowledge includes motives that other people cannot observe or reliably judge.

phrases.translation: There is no moving creature on earth whose provision is not guaranteed by Allah. And He knows where it lives and where it is laid to rest. All is ˹written˺ in a perfect Record
phrases.explanation: Every moving creature receives provision from Allah. The verse emphasizes His care across all living beings, not only people with wealth or social importance. Allah knows where each creature lives and where it will rest. No part of creation is outside His awareness, even when its whereabouts are unknown to others. Everything is recorded in a perfect Record. The verse combines care and accountability: Allah knows each creature’s needs and every detail of its existence.

phrases.translation: He is the One Who created the heavens and the earth in six Days—and His Throne was upon the waters—in order to test which of you is best in deeds.
phrases.explanation: Allah created the heavens and earth in six Days, with His Throne upon the waters. The verse presents creation as deliberate and ordered, under the authority of its Creator. Life is a test to reveal who acts best. The measure is not simply how much a person does, but the quality and faithfulness of their conduct.

phrases.translation: And if you ˹O Prophet˺ say, “Surely you will ˹all˺ be raised up after death,” the disbelievers will certainly say, “That is nothing but pure magic!”
phrases.explanation: The Prophet’s message includes resurrection after death. The verse reports that disbelievers dismiss this claim as magic rather than consider the accountability it implies. Calling resurrection magic does not answer the warning. The response reveals their refusal to accept that life continues beyond death and that deeds will be judged.

phrases.translation: And if We delay their punishment until an appointed time, they will definitely say, “What is holding it back?
phrases.explanation: When punishment is delayed until its appointed time, the opponents mistake delay for failure. The verse cautions that a consequence need not arrive immediately to be certain. They ask mockingly what is holding the punishment back. Their question assumes that what has not yet happened will never happen.

phrases.translation: ” Indeed, on the Day it overtakes them, it will not be averted from them, and they will be overwhelmed by what they used to ridicule
phrases.explanation: When the appointed punishment arrives, it cannot be turned away. The warning presents a point at which denial and delay no longer offer protection. They will be overwhelmed by what they ridiculed. The verse links their future distress with their earlier mockery of the warning.

phrases.translation: If We give people a taste of Our mercy then take it away from them, they become utterly desperate, ungrateful
phrases.explanation: People may receive a taste of Allah’s mercy and then lose it. The verse describes a test in changing circumstances, when gratitude is especially important. Some become desperate and ungrateful when relief is removed. Their response shows how quickly hope can collapse when it depends only on immediate comfort.

phrases.translation: But if We give them a taste of prosperity after being touched with adversity, they say, “My ills are gone,” and become totally prideful and boastful
phrases.explanation: After adversity gives way to prosperity, people may assume that their troubles are permanently over. The verse exposes the confidence that can mistake temporary relief for lasting security. They become prideful and boastful. Rather than remember their vulnerability, they may use renewed comfort to magnify themselves and forget the One who granted it.

phrases.translation: except those who patiently endure and do good. It is they who will have forgiveness and a mighty reward
phrases.explanation: Those who patiently endure hardship and continue doing good are exceptions to the despair and pride just described. They receive forgiveness and a mighty reward, showing that steady faith can withstand changing circumstances.

phrases.translation: Perhaps you ˹O Prophet˺ may wish to give up some of what is revealed to you and may be distressed by it
phrases.explanation: The Prophet may feel distressed by the opponents’ demands and consider setting aside part of what is revealed. The verse acknowledges that pressure without permitting him to alter the message.

phrases.translation: because they say, “If only a treasure had been sent down to him, or an angel had come with him!” You are only a warner, and Allah is the Trustee of All Affairs
phrases.explanation: The opponents demand a treasure or an angel as proof. Their challenge sets conditions for belief instead of engaging with the revelation already delivered. The Prophet’s task is to warn, not to satisfy every demand or control the response. This clarifies the limits of his mission amid the rejection he faces. Allah is the Trustee of all affairs. The Prophet can rely on Him with the outcome while continuing to convey the message faithfully.

phrases.translation: Or do they say, “He has fabricated this ˹Quran˺!”? Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Produce ten fabricated sûrahs like it and seek help from whoever you can—other than Allah—if what you say is true!”
phrases.explanation: Some accuse the Prophet of inventing the Quran. The verse states the charge plainly so it can be answered with a challenge rather than left as an unsupported allegation. They are challenged to produce ten surahs like it and seek help from anyone besides Allah if their claim is true. The challenge asks them to substantiate their accusation.

phrases.translation: But if your helpers fail you,
phrases.explanation: If the opponents cannot meet the challenge, they are asked to recognize what that failure means. Their inability is presented as evidence that the message has a source beyond human invention.

phrases.translation: then know that it has been revealed with the knowledge of Allah, and that there is no god ˹worthy of worship˺ except Him! Will you ˹not˺ then submit ˹to Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The Quran has been revealed with Allah’s knowledge, and there is no god worthy of worship except Him. The verse connects the revelation’s origin with its call to worship Allah alone. The audience is asked whether it will submit to Allah. The question turns the argument into a choice about how to respond to the truth they have been shown.

phrases.translation: Whoever desires ˹only˺ this worldly life and its luxuries, We will pay them in full for their deeds in this life—nothing will be left out
phrases.explanation: Those who desire only worldly life and its luxuries receive the full measure of their deeds in this life, with nothing omitted. The verse warns that a person may gain what they seek now yet have no lasting aim beyond it.

phrases.translation: It is they who will have nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire.
phrases.explanation: Those who seek only worldly reward will have nothing in the Hereafter except the Fire. The contrast warns that worldly success alone cannot stand in for faith and moral purpose.

phrases.translation: Their efforts in this life will be fruitless and their deeds will be useless
phrases.explanation: Their efforts in this life prove fruitless in the lasting sense. What appears valuable for a time cannot secure the reward they neglected to seek. Their deeds will be useless in the Hereafter. The verse asks people to consider not only what an action gains now, but whether it has enduring value.

phrases.translation: ˹Can these people be compared to˺ those ˹believers˺ who stand on clear proof from their Lord, backed by ˹the Quran as˺ a witness from Him,
phrases.explanation: The verse contrasts people who stand on clear proof from Allah with those who reject it. The Quran is described as a confirming witness from Him, not merely a personal opinion.

phrases.translation: and preceded by the Book of Moses ˹which was revealed˺ as a guide and mercy?
phrases.explanation: The Book of Moses is recalled as an earlier guide and mercy. The reference places the Quran within a history of revelation rather than presenting its call as entirely unfamiliar.

phrases.translation: It is those ˹believers˺ who have faith in it. But whoever from the ˹disbelieving˺ groups rejects it, the Fire will be their destiny. So do not be in doubt of it. It is certainly the truth from your Lord, but most people do not believe
phrases.explanation: Believers accept the revelation, while rejecting groups face the Fire. The contrast describes different responses to guidance and their serious consequences. The Prophet is told not to doubt that the message is true and comes from his Lord. This reassurance addresses opposition without suggesting that the Prophet himself lacks faith. Most people do not believe. The verse acknowledges widespread rejection while reaffirming the truth of the revelation and the importance of responding to it.

phrases.translation: Who does more wrong than those who fabricate lies against Allah?
phrases.explanation: The verse asks who could be more unjust than people who invent lies about Allah. False religious claims are treated as a grave wrong because they misrepresent the One people are called to worship.

phrases.translation: They will be brought before their Lord, and the witnesses will say, “These are the ones who lied against their Lord.” Surely Allah’s condemnation is upon the wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: They will be brought before Allah, where witnesses identify them as liars against their Lord. The scene makes hidden falsehood public at the final judgment. Allah’s condemnation is upon wrongdoers. The statement emphasizes the seriousness of injustice and falsehood rather than treating them as harmless speech.

phrases.translation: who hinder ˹others˺ from Allah’s Path, striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked, and disbelieve in the Hereafter
phrases.explanation: The wrongdoers hinder others from Allah’s path, try to make it appear crooked, and disbelieve in the Hereafter. Their conduct combines obstruction, distortion, and denial of accountability. Their efforts to redirect others do not make the path itself crooked. The verse exposes the deliberate attempt to discourage guidance and escape the judgment that follows life.

phrases.translation: They will never frustrate Allah on earth, and they will have no protector besides Allah.
phrases.explanation: The wrongdoers cannot frustrate Allah on earth. Human schemes may cause harm for a time, but they cannot defeat His authority or prevent His judgment. They will have no protector besides Allah. The verse warns against relying on worldly allies as though they could provide ultimate safety from divine accountability.

phrases.translation: Their punishment will be multiplied, for they failed to hear or see ˹the truth˺
phrases.explanation: Their punishment is multiplied because they failed to hear or see the truth. The language describes a refusal to attend to guidance, not a physical inability to hear or see.

phrases.translation: It is they who have ruined themselves, and whatever ˹gods˺ they fabricated will fail them
phrases.explanation: Those who reject guidance ultimately harm themselves. The verse places the lasting cost on the people who choose falsehood, even if they think their actions are protecting them. The gods they invented will fail them. What they relied on for protection cannot rescue them, exposing the emptiness of worship directed to anything besides Allah.

phrases.translation: Without a doubt, they will be the worst losers in the Hereafter
phrases.explanation: The deniers will be the worst losers in the Hereafter. The description compares temporary confidence in this life with the permanent loss that follows rejecting accountability. Their loss becomes clear when judgment arrives.

phrases.translation: Surely those who believe, do good, and humble themselves before their Lord will be the residents of Paradise. They will be there forever
phrases.explanation: Belief and good deeds are joined with humility before Allah. The verse describes faith as more than a claim, including both responsible action and a modest awareness of one’s dependence. These believers will live in Paradise forever. The permanence of the reward contrasts with the short-lived advantages pursued by the rejecters in the surrounding verses.

phrases.translation: The example of these two parties is that of the blind and the deaf, compared to the seeing and the hearing.
phrases.explanation: The verse compares those unresponsive to guidance with the blind and deaf, and believers with those who see and hear. The image describes spiritual receptivity, not the worth of people with sensory disabilities.

phrases.translation: Can the two be equal? Will you not then be mindful
phrases.explanation: The two groups cannot be treated as the same when their responses to truth differ. The question invites listeners to recognize the moral importance of hearing and understanding guidance. The closing call asks people to be mindful. Reflection should lead them to act on what they understand rather than ignore the difference between truth and rejection.

phrases.translation: Surely We sent Noah to his people. ˹He said,˺ “Indeed, I am sent to you with a clear warning
phrases.explanation: Allah sends Noah to his people with a clear warning. The story begins by showing that the people receive an opportunity to hear guidance before the consequences of rejecting it.

phrases.translation: that you should worship none but Allah. I truly fear for you the torment of a painful Day.”
phrases.explanation: Noah tells the people to worship Allah alone. His warning centers on exclusive devotion rather than a demand for personal status or material reward. He fears that they will face a painful Day. The warning expresses concern for the people’s outcome and gives them a chance to change before judgment arrives.

phrases.translation: The disbelieving chiefs of his people said, “We see you only as a human being like ourselves,
phrases.explanation: The chiefs dismiss Noah as an ordinary human being. Their argument assumes that a messenger must be socially exceptional, even though being human allows him to speak directly to his people.

phrases.translation: and we see that no one follows you except the lowliest among us, who do so ˹hastily˺ without thinking. We do not see anything that makes ˹all of˺ you any better than us. In fact, we think you are liars.”
phrases.explanation: They look down on the people who follow Noah, describing them as low-status and hasty. Their contempt for the believers’ position replaces an examination of the message itself. The chiefs see no reason to consider Noah’s followers better than themselves. Their judgment rests on social rank rather than on the faith and conduct of those believers. They conclude that Noah and his followers are liars. The accusation comes after status-based dismissal, showing how prejudice can become a way to avoid answering evidence.

phrases.translation: He said, “O my people! Consider if I stand on a clear proof from my Lord and He has blessed me with a mercy from Himself, which you fail to see.
phrases.explanation: Noah says he has clear proof and a mercy from Allah that his opponents cannot perceive. His confidence rests on guidance from his Lord, not on their recognition or approval.

phrases.translation: Should we ˹then˺ force it on you against your will
phrases.explanation: He asks whether he should force the message on them against their will. Noah does not compel belief, showing that conveying truth and controlling another person’s response are different responsibilities.

phrases.translation: O my people! I do not ask you for a payment for this ˹message˺.
phrases.explanation: Noah asks for no payment for delivering the message. His work is not a means of gaining wealth, so the people cannot dismiss it as a scheme for personal profit.

phrases.translation: My reward is only from Allah. And I will never dismiss the believers, for they will surely meet their Lord. But I can see that you are a people acting ignorantly
phrases.explanation: Noah’s reward is from Allah alone. The statement emphasizes sincerity and keeps the focus on the message rather than on what the messenger might gain from his people. He refuses to dismiss the believers because they will meet their Lord. Their lower social standing does not make their faith less important or justify treating them unjustly. Noah says the chiefs are acting ignorantly. Their demand to exclude believers reveals a failure to understand that all people will answer to Allah.

phrases.translation: O my people! Who would protect me from Allah if I were to dismiss them? Will you not then be mindful
phrases.explanation: Noah asks who could protect him from Allah if he dismissed the believers. The question shows that accommodating the chiefs by wronging the faithful would itself be a serious offense.

phrases.translation: I do not say to you that I possess Allah’s treasuries or know the unseen,
phrases.explanation: Noah does not claim access to Allah’s treasuries, knowledge of the unseen, or angelic status. He rejects exaggerated claims about himself and speaks honestly about the limits of his role.

phrases.translation: nor do I claim to be an angel, nor do I say that Allah will never grant goodness to those you look down upon. Allah knows best what is ˹hidden˺ within them. ˹If I did,˺ then I would truly be one of the wrongdoers.”
phrases.explanation: He will not claim that Allah withholds goodness from people the chiefs despise. Their social contempt does not allow them to decide who may receive Allah’s favor. Allah knows what is hidden within the believers. Noah leaves judgment of their inner state to Allah rather than accepting the chiefs’ status-based assessment. If Noah made false claims, he would be among the wrongdoers. His statement underscores honesty and refuses to use authority he does not possess.

phrases.translation: They protested, “O Noah! You have argued with us far too much, so bring upon us what you threaten us with, if what you say is true.”
phrases.explanation: Noah’s people complain that he has argued with them for too long. Their frustration reflects their rejection of his repeated warnings, not a lack of opportunity to hear them. They demand that he bring the threatened punishment if he is truthful. Their challenge treats delay as proof against the warning, while the story shows that the timing belongs to Allah.

phrases.translation: He responded, “It is Allah Who can bring it upon you if He wills, and then you will have no escape
phrases.explanation: Noah answers that only Allah can bring the punishment, and that it happens if He wills. The messenger conveys the warning but does not control its timing. The people will have no escape when it comes. The response rejects their assumption that they can summon or avoid divine judgment on their own terms.

phrases.translation: My advice will not benefit you—no matter how hard I try—if Allah wills ˹for˺ you to stray. He is your Lord, and to Him you will ˹all˺ be returned.”
phrases.explanation: Noah says advice cannot benefit people who persist in straying. The statement recognizes that hearing a warning does not guarantee that listeners will accept it. Allah remains their Lord even when they reject Noah. Their denial does not remove His authority over them or change their relationship to their Creator. Everyone will be returned to Allah. The final return gives weight to Noah’s warning and places the dispute within a larger judgment.

phrases.translation: Or do they say, “He has fabricated this ˹Quran˺!”? Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “If I have done so, then I bear the burden of that sin! But I am free from your sinful accusation.”
phrases.explanation: Some accuse the Prophet of fabricating the Quran. This repeats the sort of accusation made against earlier messengers and shifts attention away from the revelation’s message. The Prophet says that if he had fabricated the Quran, he would bear the burden of that sin. The conditional answer rejects the charge without accepting it as true. He is free of the opponents’ sinful accusation. The verse separates responsibility for a false claim from the person who is falsely accused of making it.

phrases.translation: And it was revealed to Noah, “None of your people will believe except those who already have. So do not be distressed by what they have been doing
phrases.explanation: Allah tells Noah that no one else among his people will believe beyond those who already have. Noah is told not to grieve over their conduct, since he has conveyed the message and their response is known to Allah.

phrases.translation: And build the Ark under Our ˹watchful˺ Eyes and directions, and do not plead with Me for those who have done wrong, for they will surely be drowned.”
phrases.explanation: Noah is commanded to build the Ark under Allah’s watch and direction. The task is guided and protected by Allah, even as the people continue to reject him. Noah is told not to plead for the wrongdoers who are destined to drown. The decision follows a long period of warning and the revelation that the people will not believe. The wrongdoers will be drowned. The verse makes clear that the Ark is being built in preparation for a real judgment, not as a symbolic threat.

phrases.translation: So he began to build the Ark, and whenever some of the chiefs of his people passed by, they mocked him. He said, “If you laugh at us, we will ˹soon˺ laugh at you similarly
phrases.explanation: As Noah builds the Ark, passing chiefs mock him. Their ridicule continues even while he follows Allah’s instructions, showing how public scorn can accompany faithful work. Noah says that they will soon laugh at one another in turn. His reply anticipates a reversal in which those mocking him will face the consequences of their rejection.

phrases.translation: You will soon come to know who will be visited by a humiliating torment ˹in this life˺ and overwhelmed by an everlasting punishment ˹in the next˺.”
phrases.explanation: Noah tells the people they will learn who receives humiliating torment in this life and everlasting punishment in the next. The warning distinguishes immediate disgrace from the lasting consequences of wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: And when Our command came and the oven burst ˹with water˺,
phrases.explanation: When Allah’s command comes and the flood begins, Noah is told to take pairs from the species into the Ark. The scene moves from preparation to the event the people had dismissed.

phrases.translation: We said ˹to Noah˺, “Take into the Ark a pair from every species along with your family—except those against whom the decree ˹to drown˺ has already been passed—and those who believe.” But none believed with him except for a few
phrases.explanation: Noah is also to take his family, except those already decreed to drown, and the believers. The instructions recognize both the people under his care and the faithful who responded. Only a few believe with Noah. The small number highlights how widely the people rejected the warning despite the time they had been given.

phrases.translation: And he said, “Board it!
phrases.explanation: Noah tells his people to board the Ark as the flood begins. The command marks a transition from warning to rescue and asks the believers to trust the means Allah has provided.

phrases.translation: In the Name of Allah it will sail and cast anchor. Surely my Lord is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful.”
phrases.explanation: The Ark sails and comes to rest in Allah’s name. Noah’s words recognize that the journey and its safety depend on Allah, not merely on the vessel. Noah calls Allah All-Forgiving and Most Merciful. Even amid judgment, the verse closes with divine mercy, which has protected those who believed.

phrases.translation: And ˹so˺ the Ark sailed with them through waves like mountains. Noah called out to his son, who stood apart, “O my dear son! Come aboard with us and do not be with the disbelievers.”
phrases.explanation: The Ark moves through waves as high as mountains. The image conveys the scale of the flood and the danger surrounding those who have entered the vessel. Noah sees his son standing apart from the Ark and calls him tenderly. The separation is physical, but it also reflects the son’s rejection of the message. Noah urges his son to board and not remain with the disbelievers. His appeal shows a father’s concern, even as the son must choose whether to respond.

phrases.translation: He replied, “I will take refuge on a mountain, which will protect me from the water.” Noah cried, “Today no one is protected from Allah’s decree except those to whom He shows mercy!” And the waves came between them, and his son was among the drowned
phrases.explanation: Noah’s son believes a mountain will protect him from the flood. He relies on a visible refuge while failing to recognize that the danger is part of Allah’s decree. Noah answers that no one is protected from Allah’s decree except those shown mercy. A high place cannot provide safety from divine judgment. Waves separate father and son, and the son drowns. The tragic outcome shows that family ties alone do not replace faith or protect someone from the consequences described.

phrases.translation: And it was said, “O earth! Swallow up your water. And O sky! Withhold ˹your rain˺.” The floodwater receded and the decree was carried out.
phrases.explanation: Allah commands the earth to absorb its water and the sky to stop raining. The scene presents the end of the flood as fully under divine command. The floodwater recedes and the decree is fulfilled. The danger ends when Allah’s command has been carried out, not because the people could control the flood themselves.

phrases.translation: The Ark rested on Mount Judi, and it was said, “Away with the wrongdoing people!”
phrases.explanation: The Ark comes to rest on Mount Judi, and the wrongdoers are dismissed. The story closes the flood scene with safety for the rescued and judgment for those who persisted in wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: Noah called out to his Lord, saying, “My Lord! Certainly my son is ˹also˺ of my family, Your promise is surely true, and You are the most just of all judges!”
phrases.explanation: Noah appeals to Allah about his son, reasoning that he belongs to his family and trusting Allah’s promise. His words show his concern and his effort to understand how the promise applies.

phrases.translation: Allah replied, “O Noah! He is certainly not of your family—he was entirely of unrighteous conduct. So do not ask Me about what you have no knowledge of! I warn you so you do not fall into ignorance.”
phrases.explanation: Allah explains that Noah’s son is not included among the family promised rescue because his conduct is unrighteous. The passage makes moral response, not ancestry alone, decisive. Noah is warned not to ask about what he does not know. The instruction teaches him to accept Allah’s knowledge and avoid speaking beyond what has been revealed.

phrases.translation: Noah pleaded, “My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about what I have no knowledge of, and unless You forgive me and have mercy on me, I will be one of the losers.”
phrases.explanation: Noah seeks refuge from asking about what he does not know and asks for forgiveness and mercy. His response shows humility and a willingness to correct himself when Allah clarifies the matter.

phrases.translation: It was said, “O Noah! Disembark with Our peace and blessings on you and some of the descendants of those with you. As for the others, We will allow them ˹a brief˺ enjoyment, then they will be touched with a painful punishment from Us.”
phrases.explanation: Noah is told to disembark with Allah’s peace and blessings. The survivors leave the Ark under a promise of safety and care after the flood. Blessings are also promised to some descendants of those who were with Noah. The future community grows from the rescued people, though not every later descendant will follow the same path. Others will receive temporary enjoyment before painful punishment. The verse distinguishes short worldly provision from the final outcome of those who reject guidance.

phrases.translation: This is one of the stories of the unseen, which we reveal to you ˹O Prophet˺. Neither you nor your people knew it before this.
phrases.explanation: The story of Noah is described as knowledge of the unseen revealed to the Prophet. The framing emphasizes that this account reaches him through revelation. Neither the Prophet nor his people knew this story before the revelation. The verse presents the account as new knowledge given by Allah, rather than something already learned from their own history.

phrases.translation: So be patient! Surely the ultimate outcome belongs ˹only˺ to the righteous
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to be patient because the ultimate outcome belongs to the righteous. The story encourages perseverance when truth is rejected, since the final judgment is not determined by current power.

phrases.translation: And to the people of ’Âd We sent their brother Hûd. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah. You have no god other than Him. You do nothing but fabricate lies ˹against Allah˺
phrases.explanation: Hud is sent to the people of Aad as one of their own. This closeness makes his warning direct and familiar, rather than a message from a distant stranger. Hud calls the people to worship Allah alone. The message rejects any rival deity and begins with the same foundation taught by the earlier prophets. Hud says the people are fabricating lies against Allah. The verse identifies false claims about worship as a central wrong he is sent to challenge.

phrases.translation: O my people! I do not ask you for any reward for this ˹message˺. My reward is only from the One Who created me. Will you not then understand
phrases.explanation: Hud asks for no payment for delivering the message. His warning is not a business arrangement or a way to enrich himself through the people’s acceptance. His reward comes from the One who created him. Hud points to Allah as the source of his life and recompense, then asks whether the people will understand this sincerity.

phrases.translation: And O my people! Seek your Lord’s forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance. He will shower you with rain in abundance, and add strength to your strength. So do not turn away, persisting in wickedness.”
phrases.explanation: Hud urges his people to seek forgiveness and turn back to Allah. Repentance offers a way to leave wrongdoing rather than persist in it. Hud promises rain and added strength if the people repent. The verse connects turning to Allah with renewed provision and well-being, while making clear that blessings come from Him. He warns them not to turn away and persist in wickedness. The invitation to repent is paired with a clear choice to stop wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: They argued, “O Hûd! You have not given us any clear proof, and we will never abandon our gods upon your word, nor will we believe in you
phrases.explanation: The people of Aad claim Hud has brought no clear proof. Their statement dismisses his warning rather than examining its call to worship Allah alone. They refuse to abandon their gods or believe Hud on his word. Their response shows that loyalty to inherited worship outweighs their willingness to consider the message.

phrases.translation: All we can say is that some of our gods have possessed you with evil.” He said, “I call Allah to witness, and you too bear witness, that I ˹totally˺ reject whatever you associate
phrases.explanation: They accuse Hud of being afflicted by one of their gods. The charge attempts to discredit the messenger by attributing his warning to a supernatural attack. Hud calls Allah and the people to witness that he rejects their association of partners with Allah. His response makes his position clear and refuses to bargain over exclusive worship.

phrases.translation: with Him ˹in worship˺. So let all of you plot against me without delay
phrases.explanation: Hud tells the people to plot against him without delay. His challenge expresses confidence in Allah and shows that threats cannot make him conceal his rejection of idolatry. His confidence is not weakened by their threats.

phrases.translation: I have put my trust in Allah—my Lord and your Lord. There is no living creature that is not completely under His control. Surely my Lord’s Way is perfect justice
phrases.explanation: Hud trusts in Allah, his Lord and theirs, and says every living creature is under Allah’s control. The verse makes his confidence rest on the Creator’s authority and perfect justice.

phrases.translation: But if you turn away, I have already delivered to you what I have been sent with. My Lord will replace you with others. You are not harming Him in the least. Indeed, my Lord is a ˹vigilant˺ Keeper over all things.”
phrases.explanation: If the people turn away, Hud has still delivered the message entrusted to him. Their rejection does not undo his responsibility or make him accountable for their choice. Allah can replace the people with others, and their rejection does not harm Him. Hud warns them that they are risking their own future, not weakening Allah’s power. Allah is a vigilant Keeper over all things. Nothing in the people’s actions escapes His watch, so the warning remains relevant whether or not Hud is believed.

phrases.translation: When Our command came, We rescued Hûd and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us, saving them from a harsh torment
phrases.explanation: When Allah’s command comes, He rescues Hud and the believers through His mercy and saves them from harsh torment. Their deliverance is attributed to Allah’s compassion, not their own power.

phrases.translation: That was ’Âd. They denied the signs of their Lord, disobeyed His messengers, and followed the command of every stubborn tyrant
phrases.explanation: Aad deny their Lord’s signs and disobey the messengers sent to guide them. Their rejection is not limited to Hud but forms part of a broader refusal of prophetic warnings. They follow the command of every stubborn tyrant. The verse describes their choice to align with oppressive leaders rather than heed the messengers’ call.

phrases.translation: They were followed by a curse in this world, as they will be on the Day of Judgment. Surely ’Âd denied their Lord. So away with ’Âd, the people of Hûd
phrases.explanation: Aad are followed by a curse in this world and on the Day of Judgment. The consequences of their rejection extend beyond their lifetime and are not limited to worldly events. The surah repeats that Aad denied their Lord and closes with a dismissal of Hud’s people. Their story stands as a warning against persistent rejection and allegiance to tyranny.

phrases.translation: And to the people of Thamûd We sent their brother Ṣâliḥ. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah. You have no god other than Him.
phrases.explanation: Salih is sent to the people of Thamud and calls them to worship Allah alone. His message begins with the same foundation as Noah’s: no other deity has the right to be worshipped.

phrases.translation: He ˹is the One Who˺ produced you from the earth and settled you on it.
phrases.explanation: Allah produced the people from the earth and settled them upon it. Salih reminds them that their existence and place in the world come from Allah, not from the idols they honor.

phrases.translation: So seek His forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance. Surely my Lord is Ever Near, All-Responsive ˹to prayers˺.”
phrases.explanation: Salih urges them to seek forgiveness and repent. Returning to Allah offers a path away from wrongdoing and back toward the One who created and sustains them. Allah is Ever Near and All-Responsive to prayer. Salih’s call is paired with hope that sincere repentance is heard and answered by his Lord.

phrases.translation: They argued, “O Ṣâliḥ! We truly had high hopes in you before this. How dare you forbid us to worship what our forefathers had worshipped? We are certainly in alarming doubt about what you are inviting us to.”
phrases.explanation: The people say they had high hopes in Salih before he challenged their worship. Their disappointment shows that they valued him only while he left their inherited beliefs untouched. They object that Salih forbids the worship practiced by their ancestors. Tradition is used as a reason to resist change, rather than as evidence that the practice is true. They say they are in alarming doubt about his invitation. Their uncertainty does not make them reconsider the idols, but becomes another way to dismiss Salih’s message.

phrases.translation: He responded, “O my people! Consider if I stand on a clear proof from my Lord and He has blessed me with a mercy from Him.
phrases.explanation: Salih says he has clear proof from his Lord and a mercy from Him. His authority rests on guidance granted by Allah, not on his former standing among the people.

phrases.translation: Who could help me against Allah if I were to disobey Him? You would only contribute to my doom
phrases.explanation: He asks who could protect him from Allah if he disobeyed. Salih will not abandon the truth to win approval, because doing so would place him in danger before his Lord. The people would only add to his doom by urging disobedience. The statement warns that advice to reject Allah cannot bring safety to either the messenger or his people.

phrases.translation: And O my people! This she-camel of Allah is a sign for you. So leave her to graze ˹freely˺ on Allah’s earth and do her no harm, or a swift punishment will overtake you!”
phrases.explanation: The she-camel is presented as a sign from Allah for Thamud. Its presence makes their test concrete and gives them a clear instruction to follow. The people are told to let the camel graze freely on Allah’s earth. The land belongs to Allah, so they must not treat the animal as theirs to harm or control unjustly. They are warned not to harm the camel or a swift punishment will come. The command tests whether they will respect the sign and obey a clear boundary.

phrases.translation: But they killed her, so he warned ˹them˺, “You have ˹only˺ three ˹more˺ days to enjoy life in your homes—this is an unfailing promise!”
phrases.explanation: Thamud kill the she-camel despite the warning. Their action is a deliberate rejection of the sign and the instruction they had been given. Salih tells them they have only three more days in their homes, and calls it an unfailing promise. The short interval makes the consequence of their act immediate and unmistakable.

phrases.translation: When Our command came, We saved Ṣâliḥ and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us and spared them the disgrace of that Day. Surely your Lord ˹alone˺ is the All-Powerful, Almighty
phrases.explanation: Allah saves Salih and those who believe with him by His mercy. Their survival is not an achievement of greater force but a rescue granted by Allah. The believers are spared the disgrace of the Day of punishment. The verse contrasts their rescue with the fate of those who rejected the warning. Allah is the All-Powerful, Almighty. These names affirm that His command cannot be resisted and that He is able to protect whom He wills.

phrases.translation: And the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook the wrongdoers, so they fell lifeless in their homes
phrases.explanation: A mighty blast overtakes the wrongdoers, leaving them lifeless in their homes. The sudden end reverses the security they may have felt while ignoring Salih’s warning. The scene unfolds even among familiar surroundings.

phrases.translation: as if they had never lived there. Surely Thamûd denied their Lord, so away with Thamûd
phrases.explanation: The ruined people seem as though they had never lived in their homes. Their former settlements and presence have vanished, showing how little worldly permanence can withstand judgment. Thamud denied their Lord, and the verse dismisses them as a warning to others. Their end is tied to their rejection, not to an absence of guidance.

phrases.translation: And surely Our messenger-angels came to Abraham with good news ˹of a son˺. They greeted ˹him with˺, “Peace!” And he replied, “Peace ˹be upon you˺!” Then it was not long before he brought ˹them˺ a ˹fat,˺ roasted calf
phrases.explanation: Angels come to Abraham with good news and greet him with peace. Their arrival begins with a courteous exchange before Abraham learns the purpose of their visit. Abraham returns the greeting and quickly brings a roasted calf for his guests. His hospitality shows a welcoming response to visitors, even before he knows they are angels.

phrases.translation: And when he saw that their hands did not reach for the food,
phrases.explanation: When the visitors do not reach for the food, Abraham becomes suspicious. Their unusual behavior unsettles him because sharing a meal is part of the customary hospitality he has offered.

phrases.translation: he became suspicious and fearful of them. They reassured ˹him˺, “Do not be afraid! We are ˹angels˺ sent ˹only˺ against the people of Lot.”
phrases.explanation: Abraham feels fear as well as suspicion. The verse recognizes his natural reaction to guests whose intentions he does not yet understand. The visitors reassure Abraham that they are angels sent against the people of Lot. Their explanation resolves his fear and signals the purpose of their journey.

phrases.translation: And his wife was standing by, so she laughed, then We gave her good news of ˹the birth of˺ Isaac, and, after him, Jacob
phrases.explanation: Abraham’s wife is standing nearby and laughs at the news or moment described. The reaction introduces the surprising announcement that follows for a woman of advanced age. She receives the good news that she will give birth to Isaac. The announcement comes as an unexpected blessing after the couple’s long life together. Jacob is promised after Isaac. The news extends beyond one birth and points to a continuing family line through the generations.

phrases.translation: She wondered, “Oh, my! How can I have a child in this old age, and my husband here is an old man? This is truly an astonishing thing!”
phrases.explanation: Abraham’s wife wonders how she could bear a child at her age when her husband is also old. Her astonishment reflects the extraordinary nature of the promise, not a denial that Allah can fulfill it.

phrases.translation: They responded, “Are you astonished by Allah’s decree? May Allah’s mercy and blessings be upon you, O people of this house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy, All-Glorious.”
phrases.explanation: The angels ask whether she is astonished at Allah’s decree. The question directs her attention from the couple’s age to Allah’s power to bring about what He wills. They invoke Allah’s mercy and blessings upon the household and praise His glory. The response turns surprise into reassurance that the promised gift is within divine power.

phrases.translation: Then after the fear had left Abraham, and the good news had reached him, he began to plead with Us for the people of Lot
phrases.explanation: After fear passes and the good news arrives, Abraham begins to plead for the people of Lot. His concern for others shows compassion, even when those people are facing judgment.

phrases.translation: Truly, Abraham was forbearing, tender-hearted, and ever turning ˹to his Lord˺
phrases.explanation: Abraham is described as forbearing, tender-hearted, and constantly turning to his Lord. These qualities help explain his concern for others and his persistence in prayer. His prayers show compassion rather than indifference.

phrases.translation: ˹The angels said,˺ “O Abraham! Plead no more! Your Lord’s decree has already come, and they will certainly be afflicted with a punishment that cannot be averted!”
phrases.explanation: The angels tell Abraham to stop pleading because Allah’s decree has already come. His compassionate appeal cannot alter a judgment that Allah has determined. The people of Lot will face punishment that cannot be averted. The statement confirms the seriousness of their coming judgment and brings Abraham’s intercession to a close.

phrases.translation: When Our messenger-angels came to Lot, he was distressed and worried by their arrival. He said, “This is a terrible day.”
phrases.explanation: Lot is distressed and worried when the angelic messengers arrive. He senses that the visit will bring difficulty, though he does not yet know all that will happen. Lot calls it a terrible day. His words express dread at the danger facing his guests and the people around him.

phrases.translation: And ˹the men of˺ his people—who were used to shameful deeds—came to him rushing.
phrases.explanation: The men of Lot’s people rush to him, driven by the shameful conduct for which they are known. The verse presents their arrival as a threat to the guests and to Lot’s hospitality.

phrases.translation: He pleaded, “O my people! Here are my daughters ˹for marriage˺—they are pure for you.
phrases.explanation: Lot offers his daughters for marriage, directing the men toward a lawful relationship instead of the shameful act they seek. His appeal is a plea to choose a right course.

phrases.translation: So fear Allah, and do not humiliate me by disrespecting my guests. Is there not ˹even˺ a single right-minded man among you?”
phrases.explanation: Lot asks the men to fear Allah and not humiliate him by violating the rights of his guests. He appeals to moral responsibility and the protection owed to visitors. He asks whether any right-minded man remains among them. The question conveys his isolation as he tries to restrain a crowd determined to act wrongly.

phrases.translation: They argued, “You certainly know that we have no need for your daughters. You already know what we desire!”
phrases.explanation: The men reject Lot’s offer and say they know what he means. Their response confirms that they are not seeking the lawful alternative he proposed and dismisses his appeal. They reject his appeal directly.

phrases.translation: He responded, “If only I had the strength ˹to resist you˺ or could rely on a strong supporter.”
phrases.explanation: Lot wishes he had the strength to resist the men or a powerful ally to support him. His words reveal the vulnerability of a prophet facing a crowd committed to wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: The angels said, “O Lot! We are the messengers of your Lord.
phrases.explanation: The angels identify themselves as messengers of Lot’s Lord and assure him that his people will not reach him. Their presence changes the danger facing his guests into a moment of divine protection.

phrases.translation: They will never reach you. So travel with your family in the dark of night, and do not let any of you look back,
phrases.explanation: Lot is told to leave at night with his family. The instruction gives them time to escape before the punishment arrives. The family is told not to look back as they travel. The instruction calls for them to leave the condemned city without turning toward what they are leaving behind.

phrases.translation: except your wife.
phrases.explanation: Lot’s wife is excluded from the escape and will share the fate of the others. The verse makes clear that family connection alone does not protect someone who remains with the wrongdoing community.

phrases.translation: She will certainly suffer the fate of the others. Their appointed time is the morning. Is the morning not near?”
phrases.explanation: The appointed time for the punishment is morning. Naming the time reassures Lot that the danger is limited and that the escape must happen promptly. The angels ask whether morning is not near. Their question emphasizes that the promised event is imminent, not a distant threat that can be ignored.

phrases.translation: When Our command came, We turned the cities upside down and rained down on them clustered stones of baked clay
phrases.explanation: When Allah’s command comes, the cities are overturned and struck with clustered stones of baked clay. The verse describes a decisive judgment on the people of Lot after their persistent wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: marked by your Lord ˹O Prophet˺. And these stones are not far from the ˹pagan˺ wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: The stones are marked by Allah, and the warning says they are not far from the wrongdoers. The account is offered as a caution that injustice can carry consequences beyond one past community.

phrases.translation: And to the people of Midian We sent their brother Shu’aib. He said, “O my people! Worship Allah. You have no god other than Him. And do not give short measure and weight.
phrases.explanation: Shu’aib is sent to the people of Midian and calls them to worship Allah alone. His message begins with devotion to the Creator before addressing their conduct in trade. Shu’aib tells them not to give customers less than the proper measure or weight. Faith has practical consequences in commerce, where honesty protects people from being cheated.

phrases.translation: I do see you in prosperity now, but I truly fear for you the torment of an overwhelming Day
phrases.explanation: Shu’aib acknowledges that the people are currently prosperous. Their well-being should not make them careless about justice or assume that present comfort will continue regardless of their conduct. He fears they will face the torment of an overwhelming Day. The warning links economic wrongdoing with accountability before Allah.

phrases.translation: O my people! Give full measure and weigh with justice. Do not defraud people of their property, nor go about spreading corruption in the land
phrases.explanation: The people are told to give full measure and weigh fairly. The instruction makes justice concrete in ordinary exchange, where small dishonesties can steadily deprive others. They must not defraud people of their property. The verse protects others’ rights and rejects taking advantage of them for private gain. They are also told not to spread corruption in the land. Commercial cheating is part of a wider pattern of harm that damages the community.

phrases.translation: What is left ˹as a lawful gain˺ by Allah is far better for you if you are ˹truly˺ believers. And I am not a keeper over you.”
phrases.explanation: What Allah leaves as lawful gain is better for the people if they truly believe. Honest earnings may be less than dishonest profit, but they carry blessing and avoid harming others. Shu’aib says he is not appointed as their keeper. He can warn and advise, but each person remains responsible for choosing honest conduct.

phrases.translation: They asked ˹sarcastically˺, “O Shu’aib! Does your prayer command you that we should abandon what our forefathers worshipped or give up managing our wealth as we please? Indeed, you are such a tolerant, sensible man!”
phrases.explanation: The people mockingly blame Shu’aib’s prayer for his call to abandon ancestral worship. They treat religious practice as an intrusion rather than considering whether the inherited worship is true. They also resist limits on how they manage their wealth. The verse shows that their objection is not only religious but tied to freedom from ethical restraint in business. Their praise of Shu’aib as tolerant and sensible is sarcastic. They use his reputation to ridicule the very guidance they refuse to follow.

phrases.translation: He said, “O my people! Consider if I stand on a clear proof from my Lord and He has blessed me with a good provision from Him.
phrases.explanation: Shu’aib says he has clear proof from his Lord and good provision from Him. His own blessings do not make him corrupt, and they do not excuse the people’s dishonest trading.

phrases.translation: I do not want to do what I am forbidding you from. I only intend reform to the best of my ability. My success comes only through Allah. In Him I trust and to Him I turn
phrases.explanation: He does not want to do the wrongdoing he forbids them to commit. His instruction is not hypocritical advice imposed on others while he acts differently himself. Shu’aib’s intention is reform as far as he can manage. He seeks to improve the community rather than gain authority or wealth through the dispute. His success comes only through Allah, in whom he trusts and to whom he turns. The verse grounds reform in reliance on Allah while still requiring sincere effort.

phrases.translation: O my people! Do not let your opposition to me lead you to a fate similar to that of the people of Noah, or Hûd, or Ṣâliḥ. And the people of Lot are not far from you
phrases.explanation: Shu’aib warns that opposition to him could bring an outcome like that of Noah, Hud, or Salih’s people. Their histories show that rejecting a messenger can carry serious consequences. The people of Lot are not far away. Their fate is a nearby reminder that the consequences of wrongdoing are not merely distant stories.

phrases.translation: So seek your Lord’s forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance. Surely my Lord is Most Merciful, All-Loving.”
phrases.explanation: Shu’aib again urges the people to seek forgiveness and turn back to Allah. Repentance offers a way to leave fraud and corruption rather than defend them. Allah is Most Merciful and All-Loving. The call to repent is grounded in hope that Allah welcomes those who return sincerely.

phrases.translation: They threatened, “O Shu’aib! We do not comprehend much of what you say, and surely we see you powerless among us.
phrases.explanation: The people claim they barely understand Shu’aib. Their words can mean they refuse to accept his teaching, since he has already spoken clearly about worship and honest trade. They see Shu’aib as weak among them. The insult relies on social or political power rather than responding to the truth of his message.

phrases.translation: Were it not for your clan, we would have certainly stoned you, for you are nothing to us.”
phrases.explanation: They say his clan is the only reason they have not stoned him. The threat reveals how far they are willing to go to silence the messenger. They say Shu’aib means nothing to them. Their contempt for him becomes a way to dismiss his warning and the obligations it places on them.

phrases.translation: He said, “O my people! Do you have more regard for my clan than for Allah, turning your back on Him entirely? Surely my Lord is Fully Aware of what you do
phrases.explanation: Shu’aib asks whether they value his clan more than Allah. Their threat assumes that family protection matters more than divine authority and accountability. They turn their backs on Allah, though He is fully aware of their actions. The warning reminds them that the One they ignore sees both their threats and their dishonesty.

phrases.translation: O my people! Persist in your ways, for I ˹too˺ will persist in mine. You will soon come to know who will be visited by a humiliating torment and is a liar! And watch! I too am watching with you!”
phrases.explanation: Shu’aib tells the people to continue as they choose while he continues his own course. The statement makes clear that their disagreement will not make him abandon his duty. They will soon learn who receives humiliating torment and who has been lying. The warning turns the accusation back toward a future judgment that will expose the truth. Shu’aib says he is watching alongside them. He does not claim to control what happens, but awaits the outcome of Allah’s decree.

phrases.translation: When Our command came, We saved Shu’aib and those who believed with him by a mercy from Us. And the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook the wrongdoers, so they fell lifeless in their homes
phrases.explanation: Allah saves Shu’aib and those who believe with him through His mercy. Their deliverance shows that the people who respond to the warning are not swept away with the wrongdoers. A mighty blast kills the wrongdoers in their homes. The verse contrasts the believers’ rescue with the consequence of the community’s persistent rejection.

phrases.translation: as if they had never lived there. So away with Midian as it was with Thamûd
phrases.explanation: The people of Midian seem as though they had never lived in their homes, and the verse dismisses them as it did Thamud. The comparison makes their loss a warning to later communities.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We sent Moses with Our signs and compelling proof
phrases.explanation: Allah sends Moses with signs and compelling proof. The verse introduces another messenger whose mission will challenge the authority of Pharaoh and his chiefs. His mission continues the pattern of warning powerful rulers.

phrases.translation: to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but they followed the command of Pharaoh, and Pharaoh’s command was not well guided
phrases.explanation: Moses is sent to Pharaoh and his chiefs with clear signs. The message reaches the ruler and the officials who share power in the land. They follow Pharaoh’s command, which is not rightly guided. Their political obedience aligns them with a ruler who leads them away from truth.

phrases.translation: He will be before his people on the Day of Judgment and will lead them into the Fire. What an evil place to be led into
phrases.explanation: On Judgment Day, Pharaoh stands before his people and leads them into the Fire. The verse reverses the image of a worldly leader, showing that following an unjust ruler can lead to ruin.

phrases.translation: They were followed by a curse in this ˹life˺ and ˹will receive another˺ on the Day of Judgment. What an evil gift to receive
phrases.explanation: A curse follows Pharaoh’s people in this life and on Judgment Day. Their conduct brings consequences that persist beyond their worldly power. The verse calls this an evil gift to receive. The image contrasts their punishment with the blessings promised to those who follow guidance.

phrases.translation: These are accounts, We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺, of the ˹destroyed˺ cities. Some are still standing ˹barren˺, while others have been mowed down
phrases.explanation: The stories of destroyed cities are related to the Prophet as lessons from earlier peoples. Their history shows what can happen when communities reject their messengers. Some ruins remain standing while others have been cut down. The visible remains invite reflection, though people may pass them without learning from the past.

phrases.translation: We did not wrong them, rather they wronged themselves. The gods they invoked beside Allah were of no help at all when the command of your Lord came, and only contributed to their ruin
phrases.explanation: Allah did not wrong the earlier peoples. Their own choices brought harm upon them, so the verse rejects the idea that their punishment came from divine injustice. The gods they invoked could not help when Allah’s command arrived. The objects they trusted were powerless at the moment protection mattered most. Those gods only contributed to the people’s ruin. Reliance on false objects did not save them and instead strengthened their attachment to the path that led to destruction.

phrases.translation: Such is the ˹crushing˺ grip of your Lord when He seizes the societies entrenched in wrongdoing. Indeed, His grip is ˹terribly˺ painful and severe
phrases.explanation: Allah’s grip on societies entrenched in wrongdoing is painful and severe. The verse warns that power and long-standing injustice do not shield a community from accountability or make its crimes harmless.

phrases.translation: Surely in this is a sign for those who fear the torment of the Hereafter.
phrases.explanation: The fate of earlier peoples is a sign for those who fear the torment of the Hereafter. Their stories are meant to awaken reflection before a person faces the same kind of judgment.

phrases.translation: That is a Day for which humanity will be gathered and a Day ˹that will be˺ witnessed ˹by all˺
phrases.explanation: Humanity will be assembled on a Day witnessed by all. The gathering makes accountability public and universal, unlike the uneven justice people experience in worldly life. Everyone will witness that Day. The verse emphasizes that no one can remain outside the final reckoning or pretend that its outcome is unreal.

phrases.translation: We only delay it for a fixed term
phrases.explanation: Allah delays the Day of Judgment only until its fixed term. The delay is not a cancellation of the promise, but part of a timing known to Allah. People cannot set that date themselves.

phrases.translation: When that Day arrives, no one will dare speak except with His permission. Some of them will be miserable, others joyful
phrases.explanation: When the Day arrives, no one speaks without Allah’s permission. The scene places even speech under divine authority and shows that no one controls the proceedings. People will be divided between misery and joy. The verse introduces two different outcomes, which the following passages describe in more detail.

phrases.translation: As for those bound for misery, they will be in the Fire, where they will be sighing and gasping
phrases.explanation: Those destined for misery will be in the Fire, sighing and gasping. The description conveys severe distress and contrasts with the joy promised to the other group. Their fate is not a momentary discomfort.

phrases.translation: staying there forever, as long as the heavens and the earth will endure, except what your Lord wills. Surely your Lord does what He intends
phrases.explanation: The people of the Fire remain there as long as the heavens and earth endure, except as Allah wills. The verse leaves the final matter to His will and affirms that He does what He intends.

phrases.translation: And as for those destined to joy, they will be in Paradise, staying there forever, as long as the heavens and the earth will endure, except what your Lord wills—a ˹generous˺ giving, without end
phrases.explanation: Those destined for joy remain in Paradise, with a generous gift that has no end. The verse presents their reward as lasting and abundant, while leaving its measure within Allah’s will.

phrases.translation: So do not be in doubt ˹O Prophet˺ about what those ˹pagans˺ worship. They worship nothing except what their forefathers worshipped before ˹them˺. And We will certainly give them their share ˹of punishment˺ in full, without any reduction
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told not to doubt what the pagans worship. Their practices continue those of their forefathers, but inheritance alone does not establish that worship as true. Allah will give them their full share of punishment without reduction. The warning emphasizes complete accountability rather than an outcome diminished by their denial.

phrases.translation: Indeed, We had given Moses the Scripture, but differences arose regarding it. Had it not been for a prior decree from your Lord, their differences would have been settled ˹at once˺. They are truly in alarming doubt about it
phrases.explanation: Moses receives Scripture, but differences arise among those who receive it. The existence of revelation does not prevent people from disagreeing or responding to it in different ways. A prior decree delays the settlement of their differences. The verse places the timing of final judgment within Allah’s knowledge rather than treating delay as proof that the dispute has no answer. The people remain in alarming doubt about the Scripture. Their uncertainty persists despite the revelation and does not cancel their responsibility to seek the truth.

phrases.translation: And surely your Lord will fully pay all for their deeds. He is certainly All-Aware of what they do
phrases.explanation: Allah will fully repay everyone for their deeds and is All-Aware of what they do. Nothing is overlooked or misjudged, because the One who judges knows every action and motive.

phrases.translation: So be steadfast as you are commanded ˹O Prophet˺,
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to remain steadfast as commanded, together with those who turn to Allah in submission. Steadfastness is shared by the leader and the believers who follow him.

phrases.translation: along with those who turn ˹in submission to Allah˺ with you. And do not transgress. Surely He is All-Seeing of what you ˹believers˺ do
phrases.explanation: The command to stand firm is balanced by a prohibition on excess. Commitment to the truth does not justify crossing the limits Allah has set. Allah sees everything the believers do. His knowledge makes both perseverance and restraint meaningful, even when other people do not notice their actions.

phrases.translation: And do not be inclined to the wrongdoers or you will be touched by the Fire. For then you would have no protectors other than Allah, nor would you be helped
phrases.explanation: Believers are warned not to incline toward wrongdoers, because doing so can draw them into the same wrongdoing and its consequences. The verse cautions against lending support to injustice. If they do, no protector besides Allah will save them or help them. The warning directs them to avoid complicity rather than assume that allies can shield them from judgment.

phrases.translation: Establish prayer ˹O Prophet˺ at both ends of the day and in the early part of the night.
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is instructed to establish prayer at the two ends of the day and during the early part of the night. Regular prayer structures time around worship and remembrance of Allah.

phrases.translation: Surely good deeds wipe out evil deeds. That is a reminder for the mindful
phrases.explanation: Good deeds wipe out evil deeds. The verse offers hope that righteous action can repair the record of wrongdoing when a person turns toward Allah. This is a reminder for the mindful. The teaching is especially useful to those who reflect on their conduct and want to correct it.

phrases.translation: And be patient! Certainly Allah does not discount the reward of the good-doers
phrases.explanation: Believers are told to be patient, because Allah does not reduce the reward of those who do good. Perseverance is worthwhile even when results are delayed or unseen. The reward remains with Allah.

phrases.translation: If only there had been among the ˹destroyed˺ peoples before you, ˹O believers,˺ virtuous individuals who forbade corruption in the land—other than the few We had saved ˹from the torment˺. But the wrongdoers ˹only˺ pursued their ˹worldly˺ pleasures, becoming wicked
phrases.explanation: Earlier peoples had only a few virtuous individuals who forbade corruption, and those few were saved. The verse laments the absence of a broader group willing to oppose wrongdoing. The wrongdoers pursue their pleasures in this life. The verse criticizes making immediate enjoyment the overriding priority while corruption spreads around them. They become wicked through that pursuit. The account connects neglect of moral responsibility with the community’s deeper decline.

phrases.translation: And your Lord ˹O Prophet˺ would never destroy a society unjustly while its people were acting rightly
phrases.explanation: Allah would never destroy a society unjustly while its people were acting rightly. The verse affirms divine justice and distinguishes punishment for wrongdoing from arbitrary destruction. It rejects attributing injustice to Allah.

phrases.translation: Had your Lord so willed, He would have certainly made humanity one single community ˹of believers˺, but they will always ˹choose to˺ differ—
phrases.explanation: If Allah had willed, all humanity could have been one community of believers. The verse recognizes His power to make everyone share one faith. People will continue to differ. The statement acknowledges that human responses are not uniform and prepares for the exception of those shown mercy in the next verse.

phrases.translation: except those shown mercy by your Lord—and so He created them ˹to choose freely˺.
phrases.explanation: Those shown mercy by Allah are the exception among people who differ. The verse links human difference with the freedom to choose, rather than presenting every person as forced into the same response.

phrases.translation: And so the Word of your Lord will be fulfilled: “I will surely fill up Hell with jinn and humans all together.”
phrases.explanation: Allah’s word will be fulfilled that Hell will be filled with jinn and humans. The statement is a warning about accountability for those who reject guidance, not a claim that every person is condemned.

phrases.translation: And We relate to you ˹O Prophet˺ the stories of the messengers to reassure your heart. And there has come to you in this ˹sûrah˺ the truth, a warning ˹to the disbelievers˺, and a reminder to the believers
phrases.explanation: The stories of earlier messengers are related to reassure the Prophet. Their experiences show that he is not alone in facing rejection and that steadfastness has a history. The surah brings truth, a warning to disbelievers, and a reminder to believers. Its different purposes call people either to reconsider or to remain firm in faith.

phrases.translation: Say to those who disbelieve, “Persist in your ways; we will certainly persist in ours
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to let the disbelievers persist in their ways while he and the believers persist in theirs. The statement sets out the contrast between their choices and leaves the outcome to Allah.

phrases.translation: And wait! Surely we ˹too˺ are waiting.”
phrases.explanation: Both sides are told to wait, because the final outcome will show whose course was right. The verse answers defiance with patience rather than an attempt to force an immediate resolution.

phrases.translation: To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the knowledge of what is hidden in the heavens and the earth. And to Him all matters are returned. So worship Him and put your trust in Him. And your Lord is never unaware of what you do
phrases.explanation: Allah alone knows what is hidden in the heavens and earth. His knowledge includes realities beyond human observation, so nothing is concealed from the One who judges. All matters return to Allah, so people are told to worship Him and place their trust in Him. The return to Him makes devotion and reliance the fitting response. Allah is never unaware of what people do. The final reminder assures that every deed is known and connects the surah’s warnings with its call to worship and trust.
